Hungary has finally ditched an anti-LGBTQ+ law that's caused controversy for years

Former prime minister Viktor Orbán had sought to chip away at LGBTQ+ rights in Hungary.

Actual Article Body:

HUNGARY’S RECENTLY ELECTED government has voted to get rid of legislation that discriminated against the LGBTQ+ community under the leadership of former far-right prime minister Viktor Orbán.

The new centre-right government that beat Orbán’s party in April elections, ending his 16-year tenure, has unravelled a law that significantly restricted the visibility of LGBTQ+ people in media.

Hungary has faced international pressure in recent years over its treatment of LGBTQ+ people, including from the European Union’s Court of Justice and Irish activists and politicians.

In 2021, the Hungarian parliament under Orbán passed legislation to restrict the visibility of LGBTQ+ content, embedding into law that only over-18s should be allowed to engage with information and media that pertains in some way to LGBTQ+ people.

The law had numerous ramifications, like forcing bookshops to take books for children or teens that included characters who were LGBTQ+ off the shelves or wrap them up in plastic.

One of the country’s bookshop chains, Líra Könyv, was fined $34,000 (€30,000) in 2023 for failing to wrap up “Heartstopper”, a popular book-turned-Netflix hit featuring a relationship between two teenage boys.

The new parliament has today voted to amend the legislation to protect minors from material that can “seriously impair the child’s physical, intellectual, emotional or moral development”, removing the specific ban on LGBTQ+ information.

Related Reads
                    
                
                
                
                    Maria Walsh: Hungary's election result shows the centre can still hold in Europe 
                
            
                    
                
                
                
                    With fear and courage, Hungarians refuse to let their government beat them down

In 2025, thousands of people turned out for Budapest Pride despite the Hungarian government's attempt to ban it.                    Alamy
            

    Alamy

The Orbán government also passed legislation in 2025 restricting freedom of assembly, which it used alongside the LGBTQ+ content prohibition to ban last year’s Pride parade in Budapest.

The Journal visited Budapest in July 2025 to report on the anti-LGBTQ+ politics in Hungary – and how there was still a vibrant community in the capital holding events and working together despite the efforts to push them to the margins of society.

Budapest’s Pride parade went ahead in the face of the government’s attempted ban and threats to prosecute participants and organisers, amassing its largest-ever crowd.
